LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST WORDS: FOOD & HOME · AGES 12–18 MONTHS

Shoe — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Every outing has a costume change, and the doormat is the stage. This card names the shoe at the exact moment feet become outdoor feet.

What is this?

A shoe is the foot’s going-out gear, and at 12–18 months it is a daily costume change: shoes on to leave, shoes off at home. The card shows a shoe; the doormat supplies the stage, twice a day or more.

What does it mean?

Shoe is a routine word with feelings attached: shoes mean outings, and outings mean the park, the ducks, the world. Words loaded with anticipation get said early — the front door is a motivation machine.

What does the child need to know?

Say the word as each shoe lands on its foot: "One shoe... two shoes!" The chant makes it rhythmic, and the counting sneaks in free. Then let your toddler’s own "shoe" at the doormat — if it comes — be celebrated like the headline it is.

Why this matters

Routine words have perfect timing, built-in rehearsal and real consequences: shoes on means going out. Your toddler is not just learning a noun; they are learning that words live on transitions, which is where most of a day’s drama happens.

What it teaches

Routine vocabulary at transitions, one-two counting through dressing, walking skill (new shoes, new ground), and spontaneous naming at meaningful moments.

Words to learn

shoefootonoffwalkout

Say this to your child

“"Shoe! One shoe, two shoes — on they go. Shoe on the left foot, shoe on the right foot. Stand up, little one — shoes mean outside! Off we go, walk, walk, walk. And at home: shoes off, toes free, all done."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card in the morning, shoes already in view: "Shoe. Shoes on — we are going out."
  2. Say the word as each shoe lands on its foot: "One shoe... two shoes!" Slow, chanted, unhurried.
  3. Point at the card’s shoe, then the wearing ones: "Shoe and shoe." The match completes itself.
  4. At the doormat, say the word once more — "shoes!" — and let the outing begin; the word now carries the whole adventure.
  5. Coming home, run it in reverse: "Shoes off!" Endings of routines are their own lessons, and this one happens at your door.

Look closer at the picture

The artwork is a shoe, plain and clear on the card — the going-out kind, small and familiar. Say that, then look down: the live shoes are being worn by the actual critic, and the fitting is the show.

Ask your child

Watch the doormat across the week: does the word, a point or a lifted foot arrive at the shoes? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if the shoes or the outing is the real attraction."

What your child can say or do

"Shoe!" announced at the doormat, one foot offered grandly for fitting, the card carried to the shoe rack for matching, or both shoes carried around the house as luggage — the word travelling with the object is the milestone.

Out in the real world

Shoes run through every day: on to leave, off to arrive, the tiny pairs at the shop, the big pairs by your bed. Each changeover is a showing of this card.

Try it together

Shoe parade: line up three pairs at the door, name each pair, and let your toddler choose the day’s pair by handing one over. Choosing by naming is decision-making with vocabulary attached.

Understanding check

Parent self-check: did the word land at a real transition this week, and did you cheer any doormat attempt? Transitions are this word’s home ground; the cheering is the amplifier.

Parent tips

Dressing battles and vocabulary lessons are separate events — if the shoes are a fight today, name them and move on. The word does not need the cooperation of the foot it describes.

Staying safe

Check the fit often — new walkers outgrow shoes in weeks — and slow the doormat changeover: loose laces, too-big shoes and rushing all trip new walkers. Keep the card in your hand until the feet are done.

This lesson pairs with the Shoe flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).
